newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Three plead innocent in Brazil massacre trial.
newsitem.headline: Three plead innocent in Brazil massacre trial.

text.p: Two police officers and another man pleaded not guilty on Monday to charges of killing eight street children and wounding six in a shooting spree near a Rio de Janeiro church more than three years ago.

Lieutenant Marcelo Ferreira Cortes, police officer Claudio Luiz Andrade dos Santos and locksmith Jurandir Gomes de Franca told a Rio de Janeiro state court they were mistakenly identified by street children who survived the massacre.

Six children died when men opened fire indiscriminately on about 70 children playing or sleeping on the steps of the Candelaria Church early on July 23, 1993. Two others were killed earlier and left at a nearby site, and six children were injured in the shooting spree.
Two former police officers, Marcus Vinicius Borges Emmanuel and Nelson Oliveira dos Santos Cunha, who confessed their part in the massacre, were convicted.
But human rights activists feared justice would not be done in spite of the trials and convictions.

Yvonne Bezerra de Melo, an artist who has worked with the Candelaria street children since before the massacre, said the three men on trial were likely to be declared innocent even though Cortes was named as one of the killers by key witness, Wagner dos Santos.

"No one believes what he (Santos) says. The police says street children don't tell the truth, so what's the point of Santos being here," Melo said. "This is what happens with all these types of trials; the street children lie and the police tells the truth."
Santos, 24, who survived the massacre, refused to testify at the latest Candelaria trial because he felt the testimony of Cunha and Emmanuel was being taken more seriously than his.

Cunha and Emmanuel said Cortes did not take part in the shooting spree. Another police officer, Carlos Jorge Liaffa, who Santos also identified as one of the killers, was never charged because Cunha and Emmanuel said he did not take part.

Melo also deplored the fact that Emmanuel and Cunha were not imprisoned despite receiving several life sentences, but were only confined to police barracks while their appeals proceeded. They can appeal several times until the sentences are reduced to 30 years, the maximum anyone can serve under Brazilian law.
